entities.summary:
Alfa-Bank is Russia's largest private commercial bank, founded in 1990 by Mikhail Fridman and other oligarchs as one of the first private banks permitted under Soviet perestroika, and part of the Alfa Group conglomerate. Alfa-Bank survived Russia's 1998 financial crisis and multiple subsequent crises to become Russia's dominant private bank, distinguished by its relative independence from state ownership compared to state-owned Sberbank, VTB, and Gazprombank.

Alfa-Bank's founding in 1990 coincided with the late Soviet liberalization of private enterprise. Mikhail Fridman, along with partners Petr Aven and German Khan, built Alfa Group into one of Russia's most powerful business conglomerates, including the TNK-BP oil joint venture (sold to Rosneft for $28 billion in 2013) and telecommunications assets. Alfa-Bank's management of Russian oligarch wealth and its connections to international banking created a complex network of global financial relationships.

The 2022 Ukraine invasion and resulting Western sanctions created Alfa-Bank's greatest challenge: Fridman (a Ukrainian-born Jewish oligarch), Aven, and Khan were sanctioned by the EU and UK, and Alfa-Bank was cut off from SWIFT and international correspondent banking. The bank was forced to operate primarily domestically. The sanctions raised questions about whether Alfa-Bank's oligarch ownership could survive within Russia's war economy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alfa-Bank's history as Russia's largest private bank — founded in the last gasp of Soviet perestroika and navigating five major Russian financial crises — illustrates how private enterprise survived within Russia's predominantly state-controlled banking system.
